title: Hafiz of Shiraz
hookLine: the poet of Shiraz, whose Divan many families keep by the Qur'an
tomorrow: a king asks a poet to pray for him. what does the poet say?

lines: HAFIZ: ONE WHO KNOWS IT BY HEART.
cards: Most homes have a shelf where only certain things go: a wedding photo, a grandmother's ring, the good dishes.
In some Muslim homes from Iran to South Asia, one shelf holds two books side by side: the Qur'an, and the Divan, the collected poems, of Hafiz of Shiraz. Part of the reason is in his name.
Hafiz is a title: one who has memorized the Qur'an. He took it as his pen name, and his poems say he knew it by heart. And readers gave him another name: the tongue of the unseen.

teach.h: A ROSE, A NIGHTINGALE, A BREEZE.
teach.b: Open the Divan and it reads like a garden at dawn. A rose, and a nightingale singing to it all night. The morning breeze carrying the scent of someone far away.
A cup passed around before sunrise.
Hafiz builds with the senses, smell, sound, taste, and then uses them to point at what the senses can't reach. That's why the name stuck: the tongue of the unseen.
His lines seem to speak to exactly what you're carrying, as if he knew.

teach.h: THE WINE: GOD'S LOVE, OR WINE?
teach.b: Readers have long argued over what his wine means. Some read the cup as the heart's taste of God, the beloved as the divine, the tavern as the place where pride gets left at the door.
Others read some poems closer to the ground, a man of Shiraz who loved his city, its gardens and its people. Both readings have defenders, and the poems hold both.
One thing is clear for the families who shelve him there: the Divan is poetry, honored and loved.

teach.h: BESIDE THE QUR'AN, NOT IN ITS PLACE.
teach.b: It sits beside the Qur'an, not in its place.
A scent can bring back a person you can't see. Hafiz writes like that.

how: In Iran and among Persian readers elsewhere, families keep the Divan of Hafiz at home, read and sing his ghazals, and recite them at gatherings; some open it at random for a line to reflect on, a custom scholars view differently.

a king of Persia known for his gardens of roses
a Persian poet whose name means he knew the Qur'an by heart

games.q: you read a friend a Hafiz line about a cup at dawn. she doesn't drink, and frowns. what's the fuller picture?
o: readers differ: some hear God's love in the cup, some read it closer to literal.
it's just about drinking, so she's right to put the book down.
the wine is a secret code with one fixed meaning all scholars accept.
games.why: Hafiz's wine has long been read more than one way, and the poems hold both readings.

practice: Find something near you with a scent: tea, a spice jar, a flower, even a bar of soap. Breathe it in slowly, three times, and notice what it brings back, a place, a kitchen, a face you can't see right now.
Let that unseen thing sit with you for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: Hafiz of Shiraz: the Persian poet whose name means one who knows the Qur'an by heart, and whose Divan uses the senses to point at the unseen.

orig.note: Arabic: lisan al-ghayb, the tongue of the unseen; a name readers gave Hafiz.

carryVoice: A line to carry: the tongue of the unseen, a rose that points past itself. Poets, two of six.
